rows.name: newer-focus
rows.question: Switch to transactions. Why can snapshot isolation permit write skew when concurrent transactions update different rows? Give a concrete two-doctor example.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch to transactions. Why can snapshot isolation permit write skew when concurrent transactions update different rows? Give a concrete two-doctor example.
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot and typically rejects concurrent writes to the same row, but it doesn’t prevent write skew across different rows.

Suppose Alice and Bob are both on call, and at least one doctor must remain on call. Two concurrent transactions each read that both doctors are on call. One sets Alice off call; the other sets Bob off call. Because they update different rows, both can commit, leaving nobody on call and violating the rule.

Serializable isolation would prevent both from committing successfully; alternatively, both transactions can lock a shared guard row before checking and updating.

review.note: Consistent snapshots and only same-row write conflict allow two count-two snapshots and disjoint own-row off updates; serial order/shared guard prevents both off.
review.usefulPrefix: Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot and typically rejects concurrent writes to the same row, but it doesn’t prevent write skew across different rows.

rows.name: explicit-finalized-request
rows.question: Explain why the compare_exchange_weak retry loop in the exact counter code above must recompute its desired value after failure. Give a concrete competing-update trace and distinguish spurious failure from overflow.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Explain why the compare_exchange_weak retry loop in the exact counter code above must recompute its desired value after failure. Give a concrete competing-update trace and distinguish spurious failure from overflow.
rows.answer:
Each attempt computes desired as expected + 1. On failure, compare_exchange_weak overwrites expected with the observed counter value, so the next attempt must recompute desired from that updated value.

Concrete trace: our thread reads expected = 5 and computes desired = 6. Another thread increments the counter to 6. Our CAS fails and updates expected to 6. The retry must request 7. Reusing desired = 6 could successfully replace 6 with 6, losing our increment.

A spurious failure can occur even when the counter equals expected; it performs no write, and the loop retries. Overflow is different: unsigned addition wraps at the type’s maximum. Under the stated assumptions, overflow cannot occur here; the final value is 800000.

review.note: Actual trace5->competing6->failedCASexpected6->desired7 explains why reusing6 loses an increment. Spurious failure performs no write; unsigned overflow excluded by specified range. Explicit finalized request accepted independently of acoustic quiet delay.
review.usefulPrefix: Each attempt computes desired as expected + 1. On failure, compare_exchange_weak overwrites expected with the observed counter value, so the next attempt must recompute desired from that updated value.
